source: Ackerman and Thompson (2017) Meta-reasoning: monitoring and control of thinking and reasoning
finding: Framework: initial judgment of solvability, feeling of rightness (FOR) on the first answer, intermediate confidence, final confidence, and a decision to give up. A strong FOR means little rethinking and few answer changes. A weak FOR means longer rethinking and more changes.
numbers: Review with few raw numbers. Final confidence at the point of stopping can be as low as 20% in studies that allowed opting out.
quote: When the Feeling of Rightness is strong, it is a signal that further reconsideration is not required
limits: The framework is explicitly extended beyond dual-process theory to single-process and parallel accounts.
agent_relevance: G1: doubt only on signal. The signal should be cheap to compute from the first answer (fluency, agreement), and rethinking effort should scale with it.

source: Ackerman and Thompson (2017) - cue section: fluency and familiarity
finding: Fluency (how fast an answer comes to mind) is a pervasive cue to certainty, even when it does not track correctness. Familiar material and primed familiarity raise FOR. Some cues are valid, so the fix is calibration, not ignoring them.
numbers: Qualitative summary across studies. Delaying the link between problem and solution can break the fluency-accuracy link.
limits: Cue validity depends on the task: cues that work on recall can mislead on trick problems.
agent_relevance: Do not use 'I answered quickly' or 'this looks familiar' as the doubt trigger without checking the cue is valid for this task class. Prefer code-computed signals (sample agreement).

source: Ackerman and Thompson (2017) - when reasoning stops too late
finding: Reasoners often keep gathering information past the point it helps, even paying for useless information, because more information raises confidence. Stopping is set by a confidence criterion, not by value of information.
numbers: Cited work: Ackerman (2014) Diminishing Criterion Model; Moran et al. (2015) post-choice evidence still raises confidence.
limits: Review level only; the primary papers were not opened.
agent_relevance: Stop rule for S6: stop when a criterion is met AND extra samples stop changing the answer. Add a cap, because extra thinking can inflate confidence without raising accuracy.

source: Ackerman and Thompson (2017) - individual differences and moderators
finding: Monitoring accuracy differs across people. Low performers overestimate and high performers underestimate. Sex and culture are listed as moderators. Resolution (telling right from wrong) is separable from mean confidence and goes with better performance. Feedback on confidence accuracy can improve test performance.
numbers: No pooled numbers; points to cited studies on resolution and on feedback tools.
limits: Review level; culture and sex effects are listed as open questions.
agent_relevance: Calibrate the agent's trigger on resolution (does the signal separate right from wrong on this task class), not on a mean confidence.

source: Ball and Richardson (2025) Metareasoning: theoretical and methodological developments (editorial)
finding: Special issue editorial: FOR-style triggers are now studied across CRT, base-rate and syllogism tasks. De Neys (2023) argues that two competing Type 1 intuitions (heuristic vs logical) create the conflict that triggers Type 2, so the first response may already be logically correct.
numbers: No pooled effect size. Summarises Mata (2023), Ferreira et al. (2022), Valerjev and Dujmovic (2023), Law et al. (2022), Morsanyi and Hamilton (2023), Stanovich and Toplak (2023).
limits: A rival to the default-interventionist account; the editorial says the debate is open.
agent_relevance: The first answer is not only a trap to overturn. Treat it as a candidate with a measurable chance of being right.

source: Ball and Richardson (2025) - rule-inadequate base-rate problems (Ferreira et al. 2022)
finding: Four experiments: people showed conflict sensitivity (slower, less confident) on base-rate problems even when the base rate was made irrelevant. They did not tell real from spurious conflict, so deliberate rule use can itself be an error (overgeneralisation).
numbers: 4 experiments as summarised in the editorial; sample sizes not given there.
limits: Secondary summary only.
agent_relevance: Doubt signals can fire on false alarms. G1 needs a check that the doubt is about the actual answer and not a surface conflict.

source: Ball and Richardson (2025) - Stanovich and Toplak (2023) on actively open-minded thinking
finding: Actively open-minded thinking scales predict heuristics-and-biases performance (decoupling, postponing closure) but do not predict reduced myside bias.
numbers: New 13-item AOT scale; no effect sizes in the editorial.
limits: Disposition measures do not remove every bias; myside bias is the stated exception.
agent_relevance: A prompt telling the agent to be open-minded will not fix self-serving evidence checks. Use code-side checks on evidence selection.

source: Ball and Richardson (2025) - Morsanyi and Hamilton (2023), autism and cognitive reflection
finding: With the 6-item CRT-Long, autistic and neurotypical groups gave identical proportions of intuitive and analytic answers in two age groups; analytic answers rose with age.
numbers: Editorial summary only. A different study found more deliberative answers in autism (see Brosnan and Ashwin below).
limits: Conflicting results across groups and instruments.
agent_relevance: Reflection tendencies vary by instrument; do not assume one trigger threshold fits all item types.

source: Mata (2023) Overconfidence in the Cognitive Reflection Test, Study 1 (N=60)
finding: Incorrect CRT answers carried confidence as high as correct general-knowledge answers. Global overconfidence on the CRT, underconfidence on general knowledge (GK).
numbers: N=60 (59 finished), Heidelberg. CRT correct 1.86 of 3 (SD 1.06); GK 6.64 of 10. Estimated CRT 2.41 vs actual 1.86, t(58)=4.65, d=0.61. GK estimated 5.92 vs 6.64, d=0.38. Confidence (1-9): CRT correct 8.49, CRT wrong 6.82, GK correct 7.11, GK wrong 4.35. Discrimination (correct vs wrong): CRT d=0.47, GK d=1.24.
quote: incorrect responses to CRT problems are produced with approximately the same level of confidence as correct responses to GK questions
limits: Small lab sample; percent correct was matched across the two tests.
agent_relevance: Wrong answers to trap problems are held with confidence above the scale midpoint, so a self-rated confidence trigger will under-fire on the items that need it.

source: Mata (2023) Overconfidence in the CRT, Studies 2-4: conflict is the cause
finding: Using conflict vs no-conflict versions of the same problems, overconfidence of wrong answerers was larger when an intuitive wrong answer exists. Samples were German, US and Portuguese, lab and online. In Studies 3-4 the wrong-conflict answers were not as confident as correct no-conflict answers, unlike Studies 1-2.
numbers: Four studies in total. Cited elsewhere in the paper: wrong answerers on conflict items often report very high confidence (up to 85% or 91.5% in De Neys 2013 and Johnson 2016).
limits: Boundary: the 'as confident as correct GK' result appears in Studies 1-2 only. Conflict sensitivity (lower confidence on conflict than no-conflict items) exists but is weak in absolute terms.
agent_relevance: The doubt signal is relative. Compare confidence on this item against a base for the same item class, not against a fixed threshold.

source: Trippas, Thompson and Handley (2017) When fast logic meets slow belief
finding: Default-interventionist vs parallel processing of belief and logic. Result favoured parallel: for the simplest problems (modus ponens) belief judgments were less accurate than validity judgments and belief interfered more; at medium complexity interference was symmetrical; at the most complex, belief interfered more with validity judgments.
numbers: Two experiments; deductive problems at three complexity levels (modus ponens; modus tollens and single-model syllogisms; three-term multiple-model syllogisms). Effect sizes not extracted.
limits: Contradicts the idea that a fast belief response always comes first and pre-empts logic. Direction depends on relative processing demands.
agent_relevance: A rival theory with a discriminating experiment: fast does not always mean heuristic. Do not hard-code 'first answer is the biased one'.

source: Moderate base-rate conflict detection study (2023, Journal of Intelligence)
finding: Extended 'flawless' conflict detection from extreme to moderate base-rate tasks. Biased (stereotypical) responders to conflict problems were slower, less confident and slower to register reduced confidence than responders to no-conflict problems, regardless of scale.
numbers: Statistics not extracted this session. Authors control for 'storage failure' (neutral problems show nearly everyone holds the base-rate rule).
limits: Supports the hybrid view (two competing Type 1 intuitions); authors say the study cannot locate the source of conflict.
agent_relevance: Biased answerers do sense conflict, so the failure is in acting on the doubt. The harness should turn a weak doubt into an explicit check.

source: Conflict detection with invalid inferences: all heuristics, no logic (2025)
finding: Two experiments (total N=248) on conditional inferences. 'Reverse' detection effects on invalid items vanished when items were scored by what participants chose. Invalid AC and DA inferences are intuitively valid to many people, so conflict is between two heuristics, not logic vs heuristic.
numbers: Total N=248. No reaction time or confidence difference between valid and invalid items once believability and chosen response were controlled.
limits: Boundary: conflict detection is less reliable for syllogistic and conditional reasoning than for base-rate and CRT items.
agent_relevance: A signal based on objective correctness can mislead. Measure subjective conflict (disagreement among the model's own candidate answers).

source: Law, Stankov and Kleitman (2022) I choose to opt out of answering
finding: Giving up is a stable trait across three opt-out tests. The giving-up factor was unrelated to the confidence factor, correlated positively with cognitive ability, and weakly with rational decision style and academic performance.
numbers: N=176. Giving-up with confidence r=.04 (ns). Giving-up with cognitive ability r=.26. Confidence with ability r=.61. Three-factor model fit best.
limits: Low confidence did not predict opting out more; cross-loading hints at a negative link with confidence in some task contexts. Correlations with grades are weak.
agent_relevance: Giving up is not the same as low confidence. Build a separate give-up gate (cost vs chance of solving) instead of reusing the confidence gate.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Screen inferiority in reasoning and meta-reasoning
finding: Reasoning scores were lower on screen than on paper regardless of test format. Meta-reasoning accuracy was lower on screen only in multiple-choice format. On conflict items, answer-change rate was lower on screen, read as shallower processing.
numbers: N=34 (from 38). Power analysis for d=0.25 at 90%. Answer change: question type F(1,33)=46.69, partial eta2=.586; medium x type interaction F(1,33)=13.09, partial eta2=.284; medium main effect ns (BF01=2.62).
limits: Small sample; the meta-reasoning effect depends on test format, so it is not general.
agent_relevance: The presentation channel changes how much rethinking happens. Output layout and long context could change how often the agent re-checks.

source: Brosnan and Ashwin (2023) Thinking, fast and slow on the autism spectrum
finding: Timing manipulation: autistic and control participants did the CRT in a speeded or delayed condition. Autistic group gave more deliberative and fewer intuitive answers overall. Both groups gave more intuitive answers when fast and more deliberative answers when slow.
numbers: 74 autistic and 132 control participants; fast vs slow condition.
limits: Group difference conflicts with the null group difference in Morsanyi and Hamilton (2023); instruments and ages differ.
agent_relevance: Time allowed is a causal lever on the correction rate: a protected slow pass raises deliberative answers in humans.

source: Thompson et al. 2011/2013 as restated by Brosnan and Ashwin (2023): FOR predicts rethinking
finding: Original two-response finding as restated: a low feeling of rightness goes with longer rethinking time and a higher probability of answer change.
numbers: Original effect sizes not stated in this source; the Thompson papers were not opened.
limits: Secondary citation only.
agent_relevance: This is the empirical basis for G1; verify it on our own models rather than assume it transfers.

source: Raoelison, Thompson and De Neys (2020) The smart intuitor (search summary only)
finding: Cognitive capacity predicted correct intuitive responding more than it predicted correction after deliberation.
numbers: Overall r=0.44 for correct intuitive responding and r=0.22 for correction tendency, as given in a search summary; paper not opened.
limits: Not read; numbers from a secondary snippet.
agent_relevance: Better reasoners are better at the first pass, so late correction is not where most of the gain comes from.

source: Bago and De Neys (2017) Fast logic? Time course assumption of dual process theory (search summary only)
finding: Four experiments with a deadline and load on the first answer found many first answers were already correct, fast, and confident, even against a conflicting heuristic.
numbers: No percentages obtained; the PDF could not be downloaded.
limits: Not opened. Replication status not checked.
agent_relevance: Supports keeping a correct first answer when agreement is high; do not force a rethink on every item.

source: Kadavath et al. (2022) Language models (mostly) know what they know
finding: Larger models are well calibrated on multiple-choice and true/false items in the right format. P(True) (model rates its own sampled answer) improves with size and when it sees many of its own samples. A trained P(IK) predicts 'I know' and partly generalises, but is poorly calibrated out of distribution.
numbers: Models of 800M, 3B, 12B, 52B parameters. ECE uses 10 equal-count bins. The 52B model is well calibrated except in the tails, where it is overconfident, and is biased against 'none of the above'.
limits: Format-dependent. RLHF policies are miscalibrated unless temperature is tuned. Out-of-distribution P(IK) calibration is weak.
agent_relevance: A same-model P(True) check is a usable FOR analogue when many samples are shown, but calibrate per task class.

source: Xiong et al. (2024) Can LLMs express their uncertainty? (ICLR)
finding: Verbalised confidence from black-box LLMs is overconfident and a weak failure predictor. Human-inspired prompts, sampling consistency and better aggregation help, but no method wins everywhere and all struggle on professional-knowledge tasks.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 8 tasks. Average ECE above 0.377 for GPT-3, GPT-3.5 and Vicuna. GPT-4 average AUROC 62.7%. About 22.2% AUROC gain from GPT-3 to GPT-4. White-box vs black-box AUROC 0.605 vs 0.522.
limits: 2023 models; reasoning models not tested.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on a stated confidence number. Use consistency across samples as the signal (matches G10).

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet (ICLR)
finding: Without outside feedback, a second 'review your answer' pass does not help and often hurts. Earlier positive results used oracle labels to decide when to stop correcting.
numbers: GPT-3.5 standard: GSM8K 75.9, CommonSenseQA 75.8, HotpotQA 26.0. With oracle: 84.3, 89.7, 29.0. GPT-4 standard 95.5, 82.0, 49.0; oracle 97.5, 85.5, 59.0. Intrinsic self-correction GPT-3.5: CommonSenseQA 75.8 -> 38.1 (round 1) -> 41.8 (round 2); GSM8K 75.9 -> 75.1 -> 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 -> 91.5 -> 89.0. GPT-3.5 kept its GSM8K answer 74.7% of the time; changes went more often correct to wrong than wrong to correct.
limits: Table rows read from PDF text extraction; row alignment inferred from the intrinsic table. 2023 models, reasoning tasks only.
agent_relevance: A rethink pass on every item hurts. Strong argument for G1: review only on a signal, and the signal must not be the model's own judgment of its answer.

source: Hagendorff, Fabi and Kosinski (2023) Thinking fast and slow in large language models
finding: Older GPT-3 models gave the intuitive wrong CRT answer; ChatGPT-3.5 and GPT-4 mostly avoided it, with chain-of-thought text. Instructing GPT-3-davinci-003 to reason step by step raised chain-of-thought rate from 0% to 100%.
numbers: 150 CRT tasks. Correct: davinci-003 5%, humans 38%, ChatGPT-3.5 59%, ChatGPT-4 96%. Intuitive wrong: davinci-003 80%, humans 55%, ChatGPT-3.5 15%, GPT-4 0%. Chain-of-thought in 97% of ChatGPT-3.5 and 85% of GPT-4 answers. Human check on their tasks: 38% correct vs 41% in the original study (n=3,428).
limits: Many tasks were generated automatically; models may have seen CRT items in training. Human comparison is to published norms.
agent_relevance: Writing out reasoning removes most trap errors on CRT-style items, so a visible first reasoning pass is the cheap default and a second pass is needed only on signal.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: o1-like models spend far too much on easy items. In over 92% of cases the first round of solutions already gave the correct answer, and later rounds added little diversity. Self-training that trims redundant solutions cuts tokens with unchanged accuracy.
numbers: For '2 plus 3', o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. First round correct in 89-97% across QwQ and R1 on ASDIV and MATH500. First round under 60% of tokens; on ASDIV the QwQ first round is 287 tokens, 38.7% of the response. Method cut MATH500 tokens 48.6% at equal accuracy (QwQ-32B-Preview).
limits: Math benchmarks with answer checkers; the efficiency metric needs a known answer.
agent_relevance: Supports a stop-when-stable rule: if the first answer passes cheap checks, stop. Shows the cost of rechecking without a signal.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Thoughts are all over the place: on the underthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: The opposite error: on hard items models switch between lines of thought without finishing any. Incorrect answers use more tokens and many more switches, and most wrong responses contain at least one correct thought. A decoding penalty on thought-switching tokens (TIP) raised accuracy with no training.
numbers: Incorrect responses: 225% more tokens and 418% more thought switches than correct ones. Over 70% of incorrect responses had at least one correct thought. TIP on QwQ-32B-Preview AIME2024 pass@1 38.3 -> 44.1. Dev-set grid: 35.2% to 39.8% at alpha=3 as penalty duration goes 300 to 600; at alpha=20 longer duration lowers accuracy.
limits: Gain depends on tuned alpha and duration; too strong a penalty hurts. Two models, three math sets.
agent_relevance: Two-sided: rethinking helps only when it commits to a path. S6 should say 'finish a path before switching'. A switch counter is a cheap code-side signal.

source: Fu et al. (2025) Deep Think with Confidence (DeepConf)
finding: Uses token-level confidence from the model (lowest group confidence, tail confidence) to stop weak reasoning traces early and weight votes. Saves many tokens at equal or higher accuracy, but fails where the model is confidently wrong.
numbers: AIME 2025 with GPT-OSS-120B: DeepConf@512 99.9% vs majority vote 97.0% vs pass@1 91.8%. Token cut up to 84.7% online. DeepConf-low saves 43-79% of tokens; DeepConf-high 18-59%. DeepSeek-8B AIME24 +5.8%; Qwen3-32B BRUMO25 -0.9%.
limits: Aggressive filtering (top 10%) can hurt through overconfidence on wrong problems, seen with GPT-OSS-120B on HMMT25. Needs token log-probabilities.
agent_relevance: A code-side mid-trace stop signal that beats a stated confidence. Keep a conservative setting because confident-wrong traces exist.

source: Steyvers et al. (2025) What large language models know and what people think they know
finding: Users overestimate LLM accuracy when given default explanations (calibration gap) and discriminate poorly between right and wrong LLM answers (discrimination gap). Longer explanations raised user confidence; matching the explanation's uncertainty wording to the model's real confidence narrowed both gaps.
numbers: Multiple-choice and short-answer experiments with human participants; sample sizes not extracted (abstract and introduction read only).
limits: Effect sizes not recorded.
agent_relevance: Fluent long output misleads readers. Surface the uncertainty signal explicitly in the output.
